content.value: 20. CHRISTIANITY AND CLASSICAL PHILOSOPHY

Christianity as a Creed. By the third century, the first period of interaction between nascent Christianity and classical philosophy had long been under way. But in the course of the century the new Church does not yet appear the master of the ideas it attempts to assimilate, although in other matters its achievement is already formidable. By the end of the second century the Church had organized itself in institutional forms drawn from contemporary secular society: the bishop, for instance, exercised functions analogous to those of the officers of the municipality. It had given the episcopal system a means of unified action in the form of synods of bishops, and it had based the system on an authoritative apostolic tradition, in which the position of the episcopate of Rome was already central. It had culled a canon of sacred Scripture from the mass of writings associated with the founders of the Church; and, finally, it had formulated its faith, rather than its philosophy, in brief summaries or. creeds. The importance of the creed, or rule of faith ( regula fidei ), which was professed by believers at baptism, can hardly be overestimated. It embodied doctrines to which the believer must cleave, however difficult he might find it to give them a philosophical form, should a private speculative bent cause him to make the attempt. Such a creed, in a form from which the Apostles' Creed as we know it is derived, was already a tradition in the third century in the Church at Rome. It expressed faith in One God, and in his only Son, Jesus Christ, who was made Man by being born of the Holy Ghost and the Virgin Mary; and it promised, in the doctrine of the resurrection of the flesh, eternal life to the whole man.

The Church's view of salvation maintained the infinite worth of the individual human soul, and carried with it a sense of universal brotherhood in Christ, under the rule of love. The commonwealth, taken as an ultimate standard for the behavior of man to man, was thereby challenged, and with it the idea of reason that lay at the heart of the classical conception of ethics. It is not strange, therefore, that a very complex kind of anti-secularism should have arisen at an early date. This tendency had already found expression in St. Paul, for whom the wisdom of this world was mere foolishness; and later in Justin the Martyr—whose point of view on these matters is that of a second-century convert from Platonism—and in Tertullian's attack on all the values and pretensions of the Empire. It culminates, finally, in St. Augustine's distinction between the earthly city and the City of God—a distinction which arose from reflections provoked by the sack of Rome in 410.

Our main contention is that the Christians achieved, in virtue of their faith, an independence from the premises and scheme of values of the classical world, and that they were therefore able to confront the heritage of Rome and Greece with a sense of assurance. In the third century, which we have chosen because it marks an important turning point, Tertullian was perfectly aware of the rôle played by faith in the achievement of a new attitude toward the state, history, and nature. His condemnation of reason, in its classical sense, as a source of error, confusion, and heresy, was extreme and is expressed in this characteristic pronouncement:“The Son of God was born. I am not ashamed of it because it is shameful; the Son of God died, it is credible for the very reason that it is silly; and, having been buried, He rose again, it is certain because it is impossible.” ［4］ This is a polemical overstatement of the Christian position, but it suggests to us that in the third century, from the point of view of Christianity as a faith, classicism was bankrupt both in epistemology and ethics.

The assurance characteristic of Christianity as a faith and an institution does not extend to Christianity as a body of philosophical speculation; the Christian effort to give religion an expression in terms of the prevailing philosophies of the age was, at least in the third century, in a much less happy condition than the Church taken as a whole, as an institution and a faith. The speculative effort initiated by the Apologists of the second century underwent its most trying test in its battle with the first great Christian heresy, that of the Gnostics. Its exponents in the third century, at the time of Tertullian, are Clement and Origen of the Catechetical School of Alexandria. Clement of Alexandria (d. 216) was the first head of the school; he was followed by Origen (185-254), who is perhaps the most important figure illustrating the relationship between Christianity and philosophy in the third century. We can, however, form no clear idea of the temper of the time if we forget that this is also the century of Plotinus (204-289), who gave Neoplatonism the definitive form we have already studied; for the tendencies of his philosophy dominate the philosophical tone of the age, and are especially evident in the work of Origen, who attended for a time the school of Ammonius Saccas, the founder of Neoplatonism and teacher of Plotinus.

The School at Alexandria. In the Alexandrian school, third-century Christianity is engaged in a futile effort to assimilate classical philosophy of the immaterialist sort which had long prevailed at Alexandria. This is a strain we have already noticed in St. Paul, and it is apparent in the fight of the Apologists against the extravagances of the Gnostics. Origen succeeded in supplying the framers of the Nicene creed with a formula they were able to use, but this remarkable achievement is imbedded in a Neoplatonic framework that represents a philosophical spirit quite incongruous with the faith for which Athanasius later did battle.

In Origen's treatise On the First Principles (of Christian philosophy) we recognize the culmination of the movement of Alexandrian immaterialism, which goes back to Philo. This movement includes even such Gnostics as Basilides and Valentinus, and has as its principal feature the attempt to transcend the classical dualism of form and matter by deriving all reality from a single immaterial principle. Origen's God is transcendent in the extreme sense affirmed by his younger contemporary, Plotinus: he is absolute and simple unity, beyond thought and being. In accounting for the universe of change and matter in terms of an emanation from this transcendent and immaterial principle, it is necessary to provide an intermediary; and this is the subordinate rôle assigned to Christ, who is thought of as the Logos, or the hypostatized Divine Wisdom of the transcendent deity.“He is of the same essence with God, distinct but not separate, like the sunbeam and the sun.”He is described as generated, but eternally so; there never was a time when the Son was not. But although the Son is generated of the essence of the Father, he is an eternally distinct divine hypostasis —this formula of Origen is the one that carried the day at Nicaea; he is still an inferior deity, not begotten as is the Father, but a creature. Although not in the world of change, he is close to it in that he, as intermediary, contains the germinal forms or archetypes of the multiplicity of existences belonging to the world of spirit. Of these rational existences, timelessly created by the Son, or Logos, the Holy Spirit is the highest; but, just because he is created by the Son, the Holy Spirit is inferior to him, as the Son is inferior to the Father. All these rational existences, inferior to the Holy Spirit, are immaterial souls, equal in freedom; by the exercise of this freedom some, deficient in love, declined from this original state and were imprisoned in the world of matter created for this purpose. From it they may again rise to their original spiritual state through a belief in Christ, a pure spirit. It is plain that in the Christianity of Origen's philosophy we are very far from the unified man proclaimed by the Gospel doctrine of the regeneration of the flesh, and the incarnated Christ of the Gospel is also lost sight of in this Neoplatonic philosophy.

The Nicene Creed. The Alexandrian doctrine is an expression of what from the Christian point of view is a philosophic weakness, and the continuing vitality with which classical views maintain themselves in opposition to the Christian philosophic effort bears witness to this. Throughout the third century there is a constant attack by the non-Christian Neoplatonists, and in the fourth century we find the classical reaction fostered by Julian the Apostate. It is not strange, therefore, that the development that culminates in Augustine does not derive its power primarily from the kind of speculation we have found in Origen, but from the doctrine of the Church that finds expression in the creeds, culminating in the creed promulgated at Nicaea. It is true that the Council of Nicaea utilized a formula derived from Origen; in doing so, however, it does not accept the spirit of that formula, but rather uses its words to oppose a Neoplatonism that Arius and Origen, despite their disagreement in certain important respects, both have in common. Moreover, the Council makes no effort to give its interpretation of the Trinity a speculative foundation, or to demonstrate philosophically the hypostatic union in Christ of two natures, divine and human. The sole justification of the position is in texts drawn from the Scriptures. In this respect, the fourth-century Church recognizes that its contacts with classical philosophy in the third century had been as shallow as Tertullian thought them to be. This recognition implies no derogation of the human reason, however; rather, the choice by the reason of a new starting point, or initial premise. Ultimately, the character of that very premise comes to affect St. Augustine's conception of the human reason and its workings. The peculiar relation established between faith and reason in the course of this development is indicative of the strength of the Church, whose doctrines, hitherto embodied solely in its creeds, now take on a speculative form, thereby bending the heritage of classical philosophy to its own uses.

The spirit of the Nicaean achievement is best conveyed by describing the work of Athanasius. In his writings the problem of the relation between faith and reason is not presented in terms of a sharp contrast between that which is accepted on authority, and that which is rationally intelligible. The doctrine of the Trinity is indeed a mystery, the logical explanation of which is fraught with difficulties; but its reality, its workings and power in the world around us, are self-evident to the believer. It is a first principle in that all explanation must ultimately rest on it, and it is the source of the intelligibility of all other things. The categories that had hitherto seemed adequate and self-evident to the Greek mind now lose their persuasiveness, or at least their ultimacy, and nature no longer seems intelligible unless interpreted by categories of a higher sort. Although the doctrine of the Trinity stems from a religious insight or prejudice, it is also a defensible rational position. God is conceived as the source of all existence; both form and matter are viewed as dependent on a free creative act—the source of both Being (God the Father) and Order (God the Son). The doctrine of the coinherence of the two, and of their common eternality, means that the Son is not to be conceived as a secondary demiurgic power, and that the dependence of all reality on the Father is a necessitated emanation. If the objection be made that the doctrine of the Trinity—the basic premise—is unintelligible, Athanasius' reply is that it is intelligible in the highest religious sense, though not in a narrow rationalistic sense.

Just as the universe in its entirety depends on and derives its intelligibility from the Trinity, so do man and his history. ［5］ The emphasis is once again on explanation in terms of that which is not merely an element in the context explained. A freely creating God bestows freedom, even to err, on human nature which, once fallen, can only be restored if God himself literally becomes man. For Athanasius, Scripture held that Christ was always God the Son, the Word and Wisdom of the Father, and that he became man as the son of Mary, remaining at the same time wholly God and wholly man, both in his suffering and in his miracles. Other men are potential sharers in this Incarnation; the possibility of redemption is held out to them, as unified personal existences.

The Background of St. Augustine. When we consider St. Augustine in this background, we see that he cannot be called a Neoplatonist or a Platonist without considerable qualification. In producing a philosophy which, if not systematic, yet touched on all the usual philosophical problems, St. Augustine was indebted to classicism; but his spirit is closer to Athanasius. Availing himself of classical terminology—sometimes Platonic, sometimes Aristotelian—he gives to the faith of Athanasius and Ambrose an expression in ethics, epistemology, metaphysics, and the philosophy of history. At the heart of his doctrine is the Trinity interpreted in the spirit of Athanasius. In his monumental work On the Trinity he treats it as an inexhaustible principle, accepted on faith which sheds intelligibility on the whole of reality:

For things incomprehensible must be so investigated, as that no one may think he has found nothing, when he has been able to find how incomprehensible that is which he was seeking. Why then does he so seek, if he comprehends that which he seeks to be incomprehensible, unless because he may not give over seeking so long as he makes progress in the inquiry itself into things incomprehensible, and becomes ever better and better while seeking so great a good, which is both sought in order to be found, and found in order to be sought.... Faith seeks, understanding finds.... And yet again, understanding still seeks Him, whom it finds....

The fruition of this pursuit is insight or wisdom ( sapientia ), the highest function of reason, directed toward the creative principle on which all intelligibility, including that accessible to the scientific intelligence ( scientia ), depends. The ratio scientiae turns outward, seekingto find the elements, or principles of nature, by an analysis of what is given from without. On the other hand the ratio sapientiae turns inward, finding there both God and the soul. Just as the One God is thought of as a Trinity of existence, order, and motion, so the substantial unity of the soul, a reflection of the Trinity, exhibits existence, knowledge, and will. To find the one is therefore to find the other: the self which Augustine finds, and of which he thinks he achieves a knowledge more reliable than that which he has of external nature, is both a product of and an aid toward the search for God which he undertakes under the stimulus of the doctrine of the Trinity. The contingent self, dependent on the Trinity, is therefore not wholly resolvable into its relations with a nature as apprehended by reason in the classical sense. If the self is a substance, it is so in a way that transcends external nature, much as the Trinity transcends the whole of created reality. Furthermore, the self has a status of intelligibility similar to that of the Trinity; justification or explanation of the self, or soul, is not, therefore, to be found in the world of nature. Yet in a higher context of intelligibility the soul, like God, is most knowable.

If we turn to other problems connected with man's status, similar considerations are relevant. For the ratio scientiae nature is complete, and its elements are resolvable at best into dichotomies like those between form and matter, which give rise to such problems as necessity, chance, fate, and accident. For the ratio sapientiae nature appears to be dependent upon its Creator in whom, because he is independent of that which he creates and inaccessible to the categories of the reason, and questions regarding necessity, chance, fate, and accident may be avoided. As the God apprehended in the mystery of the Trinity is not sought within nature, neither is man's status, nor the meaning of his history.

If all this involves a transformation of traditional concepts of intelligibility and of the mind's powers, it harmonizes with the notion of faith. Interpreted in this way, Augustine's dictum, “Believe in order that you may understand,”differs both from Tertullian's repudiation of reason and from the extreme dualism which opposes faith and valuation on the one hand, and reason on the other.

Many later philosophers, among them St. Thomas Aquinas, differed from St. Augustine in their account of the relation between faith and reason, will and intellect, love and knowledge, grace and nature; and their differences may well have been dictated by a desire to avoid making reason seem subservient. But the crede ut intellegas of St. Augustine prevails over the rationalistic influence of Aristotle in the thirteenth century; this century, at its height, was unable to find complete satisfaction in the classical ideal in its Aristotelian formulation. St. Thomas ascribes to faith rather than to reason his conception of a freely creative God who is a Trinity, though he would no doubt ascribe to reason alone his extension of the Aristotelian distlnction between actuality and potentiality from the restricted context of form and matter to the wider one of existence and essence. For all their disagreement St. Augustine and St. Thomas seem at one in transcending the ultimate classical dichotomy of form and matter, and it seems fair to say that for St. Thomas no less than for St. Augustine, faith in the freely creative Trinity has required a new type of first principle to satisfy the demand for a new kind of intelligibility.

There are other Thomistic transformations of the Aristotelian spirit in which the Christian faith exacts its own standard of intelligibility. Thus St. Thomas formulates an exemplarism congruent with the doctrine of the Trinity in the following passage:

And therefore we must say that in the divine wisdom are the models of all things, which we have called ideas—i.e., exemplary forms existing in the divine mind. And although these ideas are multiplied by their relations to things, nevertheless, they are not really distinct from the divine essence, inasmuch as the likeness of that essence can be shared diversely by different things. In this manner, therefore, God Himself is the first exemplar of all things. ［6］
To say this is not to suggest that the solution is not intelligible in its own right; it is only to ask whether it would have been reached without the stimulus of the faith.
